'''Murray Gerstenhaber''' (June 5, 1927 – February 21, 2024) was an American mathematician, physicist, and lawyer. He was a professor of mathematics at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], best known for his contributions to [[theoretical physics]] with his discovery of [[Gerstenhaber algebra]]. He was also a lecturer in law at the [[University of Pennsylvania Law School]].

==Early life and education==
Murray Gerstenhaber was born in [[Brooklyn]], New York, to Jewish<ref>{{cite web |title=Murray Gerstenhaber, Mathematics |url=https://almanac.upenn.edu/articles/murray-gerstenhaber-mathematics#:~:text=Murray%20Gerstenhaber%2C%20an%20emeritus%20professor,intellect%20from%20an%20early%20age. |website=University of Pennsylvania Almanac |access-date=21 October 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Murray Gerstenhaber Obituary February 21, 2024 |url=https://obits.goldsteinsfuneral.com/murray-gerstenhaber |website=Goldsteins Funeral |access-date=21 October 2025}}</ref> immigrants Pauline (née Rosenzweig; who was born in Romania; died in 1978) and Joseph Gerstenhaber (who was born in 1892 in Romania; died in 1975). His father was trained as a jeweler, "but being unable to find work in this line he [took] employment in a factory making airplane precision instruments”.<ref name=autogenerated4 /> As to his mother, in 2015 he noted: <blockquote>"For someone born into a minority family without means, I have been exceedingly lucky. The problems faced by talented but disadvantaged children today are preventing many who could be important contributors to the sciences, arts, and society in general, from achieving their potential. They don’t all have mothers like mine, who fought to find a path to education for her child. We have to seek them out but are not doing enough to find them, bring them out of isolation, and give them the opportunities I was so fortunate to have enjoyed."<ref name=autogenerated4 /></blockquote>

Gerstenhaber was a [[child prodigy]] who was profiled in [[Leta Hollingworth]]'s book ''Children Above 180 IQ'' (1942).<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hollingworth|first1=Leta S.|title=Children Above 180 IQ (Stanford-Binet)|date=1942|publisher=World Book Company|location=Yonkers-on-Hudson|isbn=978-0-405-06467-8}}</ref><ref name=autogenerated4 /> In this book, Gerstenhaber was dubbed "Child L," and his prodigious abilities and personality traits were described in great detail.<ref name=autogenerated4>{{cite journal|author1=Wigtil, C.J.|author2=White, W.L.|title=Children Above 180 IQ Stanford-Binet: A Seventy-Five Year Follow-Up|journal=Journal of Genius and Eminence|volume=2|issue=1|pages=77‒91|doi=10.18536/jge.2017.04.02.01.08|url=http://www.icscpress.com//index.php?cID=194|accessdate=August 31, 2017|language=English|issn=2334-1149|year=2017|url-access=subscription}}</ref> At age 9 years 5 months, a [[Stanford-Binet]] test showed him to have a mental age of between 17 and 18 and an [[IQ]] between 195 and 198. A second revised Stanford-Binet given a year later found him to have a mental age of 19 years 11 months and an IQ of 199+.

Gerstenhaber attended the now-defunct [[Speyer School]], a school for rapid learners in New York City. Many years later, his daughter-in-law co-founded [[The Speyer School|Speyer Legacy School]], naming the new school after the original.  After graduating from Speyer School, Gerstenhaber entered the [[Bronx High School of Science]] in 1940.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=-J4VAQAAIAAJ&q=%22murray+gerstenhaber%22+%22bronx+high+school%22 "The Cyclotron, by Murray Gerstenhaber, 16,"<!-- Bot generated title -->] ''Science Talent Research'' (1944) - Google Books.</ref> From 1945 to 1947 he served in the infantry in the [[United States Army]] as a [[corporal]] assigned to the [[Office of Military Government, United States|Office of Military Government for Germany]].<ref name=autogenerated2>[https://images.shulcloud.com/967/uploads/Administrative/VeteransProgram-2017.pdf "Our Honored Temple Beth Hillel–Beth El Veterans,"] ''Veterans Day Program'', November 11, 2017.</ref> 

Gerstenhaber finished his [[B.S.]] in mathematics at [[Yale University]] (1948).<ref name=autogenerated3>[https://www.math.upenn.edu/~mgersten/cv.html "C.V."<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> At Yale, he participated in the [[William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition]] and was on the team representing Yale University (along with [[Murray Gell-Mann]] and [[Henry O. Pollak]]) that won the second prize in 1947; each of them received a monetary prize of $30 (${{formatnum:{{Inflation|US|30|1947|r=-1}}}} in current dollar terms).<ref>G. W. Mackey (August–September 1947). [https://www.jstor.org/stable/2304390?seq=1#page_scan_tab_contents "the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition,"] ''The American Mathematical Monthly'', Vol. 54, No. 7, Part 1, pp. 400-403.</ref> His 1948 participation in the competition earned him a Top 10 ranking.

Gerstenhaber earned an [[Master of Arts|M.A.]] and a [[Ph.D.]] (1951) in mathematics from the [[University of Chicago]], under the instruction of [[Abraham Adrian Albert]].<ref name=gene>{{MathGenealogy |id=6411}}</ref> Gerstenhaber's dissertation was entitled ''Rings of Derivations''.<ref name=gene/>

Gerstenhaber earned a [[Juris Doctor|J.D.]] from the [[University of Pennsylvania Law School]] in 1973, and was admitted to the Pennsylvania bar in 1974.{{citation needed|date=May 2019}}

==Career==
Gerstenhaber was an assistant professor in the Department of Mathematics at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] from 1953 to 1958, rising to associate professor (1958–61), and full professor (1961–2024) and chairman.<ref>[https://www.nsf.gov/pubs/1971/annualreports/ar_1971_appendix_a.pdf "National Science Board, NSF Staff, Advisory Committees and Panels; Advisory Panel for Mathematical Sciences,"] ''NSF 1971 Annual Report''.</ref><ref name=autogenerated3 /> His research interests include: [[deformation theory|algebraic deformation theory]], [[universal algebra]], [[quantum group]]s, and statistics for law. He is best known for his contributions to [[theoretical physics]] with his discovery of [[Gerstenhaber algebra]].

Among his writings were ''Algebraic cohomology and deformation theory'', with SD Schack, ''Deformation theory of algebras and structures and applications'', 11–264 (1988), "On the deformation of rings and algebras," ''Annals of Mathematics'', Second Series, Vol. 79, No. 1 (Jan., 1964), pp.&nbsp;59–103, and "The cohomology structure of an associative ring," ''Annals of Mathematics'', Second Series, Vol. 78, 267–288 (1963).<ref>[https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=-Tv3m0kAAAAJ&hl=en "Murray Gerstenhaber,"<!-- Bot generated title -->] Google Scholar Citations.</ref><ref>[https://www.jstor.org/stable/1970484?seq=1/analyze "On the Deformation of Rings and Algebras,"] ''Annals of Mathematics'', Second Series, Vol. 79, No. 1 (January 1964), pp. 59–103, DOI: 10.2307/1970484.</ref> For these last two papers he received in 2021 the [[Leroy P. Steele Prize]] for Seminal Contribution to Research.<ref>[https://www.ams.org/news?news_id=6474 Leroy P. Steele Prize 2021] for Seminal Contribution to Research</ref> Gerstenhaber noted in 1990:  “The ability to hang in there has a lot to do with scientific productivity, I am convinced. And in mathematics … hanging in there is a solitary accomplishment.”<ref name=autogenerated4 />

Gerstenhaber was chairman of the [[faculty senate]] at the University of Pennsylvania from 1982 to 1983.<ref name=autogenerated3 />

Gerstenhaber was also a lecturer in law at the [[University of Pennsylvania Law School]], teaching a seminar on statistics for law.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=White, W. L.|title=Interviews with Child I, Child J, and Child L|journal=Roeper Review|volume=12|issue=3|pages=222‒227|doi=10.1080/02783199009553276|year=1990}}</ref><ref name=autogenerated3 />

In 2012 he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]], and was a member of its council.<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list "List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society"], retrieved January 19, 2013.</ref> Gerstenhaber was the managing editor of the ''Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society''.<ref name=autogenerated3 /> Gerstenhaber was also a [[Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science]].{{citation needed|date=May 2019}}

In 2021 he received the Steele Prize for Seminal Contribution to Research.<ref>{{cite web |title=Joint Mathematics Meetings 2021 Prizes and Awards |url=https://jointmathematicsmeetings.org/meetings/national/jmm2021/2247_prizes-all |publisher=Joint Mathematics Meetings |access-date=29 May 2022}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Gerstenhaber married Ruth Priscilla Zager on June 3, 1956, in the [[Congregation Shearith Israel|Spanish and Portuguese Synagogue]] in New York City.<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1956/04/29/archives/dr-ruth-p-zager-becomes-fiancee-texas-physician-engaged-to-dr.html "Dr. Ruth P. Zager becomes Fiancee; Texas Physician Engaged to Dr. Murray Gerstenhaber, Professor at U. of P.",<!-- Bot generated title -->] ''The New York Times'', April 29, 1956.</ref><ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1956/06/04/archives/dr-ruth-zager-wed-to-u-of-p-teacher-tulchinmalmud.html "Dr. Ruth Zager Wed to U. of P. Teacher,"<!-- Bot generated title -->] ''The New York Times'', June 4, 1956.</ref> They lived in [[Merion Station, Pennsylvania]], and [[Haverford, Pennsylvania]], and had three children: Jeremy M. Gerstenhaber, David Ezra Gerstenhaber (now founder, president, and portfolio manager at Argonaut Management), and Rachel Rebecca Stern (now general counsel and head of strategic resources of [[FactSet]]).<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=ILvrCAAAQBAJ&dq=gerstenhaber+murray+%22merion+station%22&pg=PA1015 Deformation Theory of Algebras and Structures and Applications - Google Books<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref><ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1994/06/26/style/weddings-rachel-gerstenhaber-alexander-stern.html "Weddings; Rachel Gerstenhaber, Alexander Stern,"<!-- Bot generated title -->] ''The New York Times'', June 26, 1994.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/research/stocks/people/person.asp?personId=25068313&privcapId=347669|title=Stocks|website=[[Bloomberg News]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/research/stocks/private/person.asp?personId=36660389&privcapId=4583454&previousCapId=4583454&previousTitle=Argonaut%20Management,%20L.P.|title = Stocks|website = [[Bloomberg News]]}}</ref> His son David, a hedge fund manager and [[Tiger Management]] alumnus, is married to financier [[Steven Posner]]'s daughter Kelly.<ref>Melanie Grayce West (June 11, 2012). [https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052702303901504577460711575300528 "Guiding Gifted Students,"] ''The Wall Street Journal''.</ref> 

Gerstenhaber died on February 21, 2024, at the age of 96.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Murray Gerstenhaber |url=https://obits.goldsteinsfuneral.com/murray-gerstenhaber |access-date=2024-03-05 |website=Goldsteins Funeral |language=en}}</ref>
